questions.stem: After discovering the electron in 1897, what atomic model did Thomson propose?
options: A nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in fixed energy shells
A cloud of negative charge with positive protons scattered evenly inside
A sphere of positive charge with negative electrons spread through it
A tiny dense positive nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance
questions.explanation: Thomson knew atoms were neutral overall, so once he found small negative particles he pictured them sitting inside a ball of positive charge — the 'plum pudding' model. The option describing a tiny dense nucleus with orbiting electrons is Rutherford's later model, proposed only after the gold foil scattering results, which Thomson did not have. The option with electrons in fixed shells is Bohr's model, later again. The cue is chronology: nucleus ideas only appear after alpha particle scattering.

questions.stem: Which gives the charge and relative mass of the three subatomic particles?
options: Protons positive, mass 1; neutrons neutral, mass 0; electrons negative, mass 1
Protons neutral, mass 1; neutrons positive, mass 1; electrons negative, near 0
Protons positive, mass 1; neutrons neutral, mass 1; electrons negative, near 0
Protons positive, mass 1; neutrons negative, mass 1; electrons neutral, near 0
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons both have a relative mass of about 1 and sit in the nucleus, while an electron is roughly 1/1836 of that mass, so it is treated as approximately 0. The tempting swap is the option giving the electron a mass of 1 and the neutron a mass of 0 — but it is the neutron that contributes mass and the electron that contributes almost none. Remember the name: a neutron is neutral, and 'neutral' refers to charge, not mass.

questions.stem: Most alpha particles passed through Rutherford's gold foil, but a few bounced back. What did that show?
options: The atom's mass is spread evenly through its volume, not concentrated
The atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
The atom is a uniform positive sphere with electrons embedded evenly
The atom has a negative centre surrounded by a shell of positive charge
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are positive, so the few that rebounded must have met something both massive and positively charged occupying a very small volume, while the majority passing through showed most of the atom is empty. The uniform positive sphere option is exactly the plum pudding model the experiment disproved — such a spread-out charge could not deflect a fast alpha particle backwards. The cue is the rare large-angle bounce: it demands concentration of mass and positive charge, not spread.

questions.stem: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron in 1932 solved a problem with the earlier nuclear model. Which problem did it solve?
options: Atoms were electrically neutral even though they contained charged particles
Electrons could orbit the nucleus without spiralling into it
Elements in the same group of the periodic table reacted in similar ways
Atoms had far more mass than could be explained by their protons alone
questions.explanation: A helium atom has 2 protons but a mass of about 4, and this extra mass was unexplained until neutrons — uncharged particles of similar mass to protons — were found in the nucleus. The option about atoms being electrically neutral is tempting but was already explained by equal numbers of protons and electrons, so neutrons were not needed for that. The cue is the word 'neutron': it fixes a mass problem, not a charge problem.

questions.stem: An unstable nucleus of radium-226 (atomic number 88) emits an alpha particle. What is the atomic number and mass number of the new nucleus formed?
options: Atomic number 86, mass number 226
Atomic number 90, mass number 230
Atomic number 87, mass number 222
Atomic number 86, mass number 222
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so emitting one lowers the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4: 88 − 2 = 86 and 226 − 4 = 222. The option keeping the mass number at 226 forgets that the four ejected nucleons take mass away from the nucleus. Check both numbers separately every time: alpha means −2 protons and −4 nucleons.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 (atomic number 6) undergoes beta decay. Which statement correctly describes the resulting nucleus?
options: It becomes boron-14, because a proton is lost from the nucleus as the electron leaves
It becomes carbon-13, because the emitted electron reduces the mass number by one
It becomes nitrogen-15, because a proton is gained while the neutron number stays the same
It becomes nitrogen-14, because a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted
questions.explanation: In beta decay a neutron in the nucleus converts into a proton plus a fast electron that is ejected, so the atomic number rises by 1 while the total number of nucleons, and hence the mass number, is unchanged. The boron-14 option assumes the emitted negative particle means a proton is removed, but the emitted electron comes from a neutron converting, which adds a proton. The cue is that beta decay always shifts the element one place to the right with the mass number unchanged.

questions.stem: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5 years. A sample starts with 80 g of the isotope. How much of the original isotope remains after 20 years?
options: 4 g
5 g
questions.explanation: Twenty years is four half-lives, so the amount halves four times: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 g. Choosing 20 g is the common slip of counting only two halvings, or of halving the 20 years rather than dividing by the half-life. Always work out the number of half-lives first (total time ÷ half-life), then halve that many times.

questions.stem: What did Bohr change in Rutherford's atomic model?
options: Electrons sit in the nucleus with the protons
Electrons spread evenly through the atom with no charge
Electrons orbit only in fixed energy levels, or shells
Electrons sit at random points in a positive sphere
questions.explanation: Bohr kept Rutherford's tiny central nucleus but proposed that electrons are restricted to particular energy levels, which explained why atoms emit light of only certain colours. The idea that electrons are embedded in a positive sphere is Thomson's plum pudding model, which Rutherford's scattering results had already disproved. The cue is the phrase 'energy levels' or 'shells' — that language belongs to Bohr, not to Thomson or Rutherford.

questions.stem: Two atoms are isotopes of the same element. Which statement about them must be true?
options: They have the same mass number but different numbers of electrons
They have different numbers of protons and the same mass number
They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
questions.explanation: An element is defined by its proton number (atomic number), so isotopes of one element must share that number; they differ only in neutron count, which changes the mass number. Saying they have the same neutrons and different protons reverses the rule and would actually describe two different elements. Remember: change the protons and you change the element; change the neutrons and you only change the isotope.

questions.stem: How are an atom's mass and volume distributed?
options: Almost all the mass is in the tiny nucleus; the electrons give it its volume
Almost all the mass is in the electron cloud; the nucleus gives it its volume
Both are concentrated in the nucleus, with the electrons contributing neither
Mass is shared evenly, but the nucleus fills most of the volume
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons are roughly 1836 times more massive than electrons, so the nucleus holds nearly all the mass, yet it is around one hundred-thousandth of the atom's diameter, so the electron region accounts for essentially all the size. The tempting reversal, putting the mass in the electron cloud and the volume in the nucleus, contradicts Rutherford's finding that most alpha particles passed straight through empty space. Link 'heavy but tiny' with the nucleus every time.

questions.stem: An unstable nucleus emits only a gamma ray. What happens to its atomic number and mass number?
options: The atomic number rises by 1 and the mass number stays the same
The mass number falls by 1 and the atomic number stays the same
Both stay the same, because the nucleus only loses excess energy
The atomic number falls by 2 and the mass number falls by 4
questions.explanation: Gamma radiation is high-energy electromagnetic radiation, not a particle, so no protons or neutrons leave the nucleus and both numbers are unchanged — the nucleus simply drops to a lower energy state. Losing 2 from the atomic number and 4 from the mass number describes alpha emission, which is a helium nucleus leaving. The cue is that only particle emissions can alter the counts of protons and neutrons.

questions.stem: A neutral atom contains 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. Which pair of values is correct for this atom?
options: Atomic number 35 and mass number 52
Atomic number 17 and mass number 35
Atomic number 17 and mass number 52
Atomic number 18 and mass number 35
questions.explanation: The atomic number equals the proton number (17), and the mass number is protons plus neutrons, 17 + 18 = 35. The value 52 comes from wrongly adding the electrons as well, but electrons have negligible mass and are never counted in the mass number. Check yourself by asking which two particles sit in the nucleus — only those two are added.

questions.stem: A sample of a radioactive isotope falls from 240 g to 15 g in 12 hours. What is the half-life of the isotope?
options: 4 hours
6 hours
1.5 hours
3 hours
questions.explanation: Halving repeatedly gives 240 → 120 → 60 → 30 → 15, which is 4 half-lives, so each half-life is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 hours. Choosing 4 hours comes from counting only 3 halvings, which would leave 30 g rather than 15 g. Always count the number of halving steps first, then divide the total time by that count.

questions.stem: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation are compared by how far they penetrate matter. Which order, from least to most penetrating, is correct?
options: Alpha, then beta, then gamma
Gamma, then beta, then alpha
Beta, then alpha, then gamma
Gamma, then alpha, then beta
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they lose energy quickly and are stopped by a sheet of paper; beta particles are much smaller and pass through paper but are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic radiation needing thick lead or concrete. The reversed order, gamma first, is tempting if you assume the most massive particle must travel furthest, but large size and charge cause more collisions and faster energy loss. Match each type to its stopping material: paper, aluminium, lead.

questions.stem: An unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle. What is an alpha particle made of?
options: Two protons and two electrons, which is the same as a helium atom
Four neutrons bound together, which is the same as a hydrogen nucleus
Two electrons and two neutrons, which is the same as a lithium nucleus
Two protons and two neutrons, which is the same as a helium nucleus
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a cluster of two protons and two neutrons ejected from the nucleus, so it is identical to a helium-4 nucleus and carries a charge of +2 with a mass number of 4. The option describing two protons and two electrons is tempting because a neutral helium atom does have two electrons, but electrons are not found in the nucleus and are not part of the emitted particle. The cue: alpha emission drops the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2, which only works if two protons and two neutrons leave.

questions.stem: Why are some isotopes radioactive?
options: Their atoms are unusually large, so they emit radiation until smaller
Their nuclei are unstable, so they emit radiation until stable
Their electron shells are incomplete, so they emit until the shell fills
They have gained extra electrons, so they emit until charge is balanced
questions.explanation: Radioactivity comes from the nucleus: a particular combination of protons and neutrons can be unstable, and the nucleus emits alpha, beta or gamma radiation, changing until a stable arrangement is reached. The option about incomplete electron shells is the most tempting because incomplete shells do explain chemical reactivity, but chemistry involves electrons while radioactivity involves the nucleus. If the question is about radiation being emitted, look to the nucleus, not the shells.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders four models of the atom from earliest to latest?
options: Nuclear, then indivisible sphere, then plum pudding, then electron shells
Indivisible sphere, then nuclear, then plum pudding, then electron shells
Indivisible sphere, then plum pudding, then nuclear, then electron shells
Plum pudding, then indivisible sphere, then electron shells, then nuclear
questions.explanation: Dalton's indivisible sphere came first, Thomson's discovery of the electron produced the plum pudding model, Rutherford's scattering evidence gave the nuclear model, and Bohr then placed electrons in fixed shells. The sequence beginning with the nuclear model is tempting because the nuclear model feels most 'modern' among the early ideas, but a nucleus could not be proposed before electrons were even known to exist. Use the evidence as the cue: each new model follows the experiment that broke the previous one.

questions.stem: During beta decay, an electron is emitted from the nucleus even though nuclei do not contain electrons. What actually happens?
options: A neutron splits into two protons, and one of them is ejected as a fast electron
A neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, and the electron produced is ejected
A proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron, and an inner shell electron is ejected
An electron from the innermost shell falls into the nucleus and is then thrown back out
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus converts into a proton, and the high-speed electron created in that conversion is emitted, which is why the atomic number rises by one while the mass number stays the same. The option about a proton changing into a neutron is tempting because it also keeps the mass number constant, but that change would lower the atomic number and would not create an electron to emit. The cue is the direction of the atomic number change: beta-minus decay always increases it by one.

questions.stem: A thorium-232 nucleus (atomic number 90) emits one alpha particle and then two beta particles. What is the atomic number and mass number of the final nucleus?
options: Atomic number 86, mass number 220
Atomic number 90, mass number 228
Atomic number 88, mass number 228
Atomic number 92, mass number 224
questions.explanation: Alpha emission lowers the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4, giving atomic number 88 and mass number 228; each beta-minus emission then raises the atomic number by 1 with no change to the mass number, returning it to 90. The answer of atomic number 88 with mass number 228 is the most tempting because it stops after the alpha step and ignores the two beta emissions. Track the two quantities separately: only alpha changes the mass number, while both types change the atomic number.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 decays in a series of steps, emitting alpha and beta particles, and the series ends when lead-206 is formed. Why does the series stop at lead-206?
options: The lead-206 nucleus is a stable arrangement of protons and neutrons, so it does not decay further
Lead is chemically unreactive, so its atoms cannot take part in any further nuclear changes
The nucleus has run out of alpha particles to emit, so no further decay is possible
Lead-206 has equal numbers of protons and neutrons, which is the condition for every stable nucleus
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay happens because a nucleus has an unstable combination of protons and neutrons; each emission changes that combination, and the series ends once a stable combination is reached, which for this series is lead-206. The option about lead being chemically unreactive confuses chemical behaviour, which depends on electrons, with nuclear stability, which depends only on the nucleus. Lead-206 also does not have equal protons and neutrons (82 protons, 124 neutrons) — larger stable nuclei always hold more neutrons than protons. The cue: if a stem asks why decay stops, the answer is always about nuclear stability, never about chemistry.

questions.stem: Elements in the same group (vertical column) of the periodic table tend to have similar chemical properties. What do their atoms have in common?
options: The same number of neutrons in the nucleus
The same total number of electrons overall
The same number of electrons in the outer shell
The same total number of electron shells
questions.explanation: Chemical behaviour is controlled by the outer-shell (valence) electrons, and every element in a group has the same number of them, so they react in similar ways. Having the same number of shells is the tempting choice, but that is what elements in the same period (row) share, not the same group. Cue: columns match valence electrons, rows match shells.

questions.stem: An atom of an element has the electron arrangement 2,8,2. What does the period (row) number of this element tell you about its atom?
options: Its atom has two full shells, so it sits in period 8
Its electrons occupy three shells, so it sits in period 3
Its outer shell holds two electrons, so it sits in period 2
Its nucleus holds twelve protons, so it sits in period 12
questions.explanation: The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells, and 2,8,2 shows electrons in three shells, so the element is in period 3. The suggestion that the two outer electrons set the period is the common trap, because that number actually points to the group (group 2), not the row. Cue: count the shells for the row, count the outer electrons for the column.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes where metals and non-metals are found in the periodic table?
options: Non-metals fill the left and central regions, metals cluster in the upper right, with metalloids along the stepped dividing line
Metals occupy the top few rows and non-metals occupy the bottom rows, with metalloids in the middle rows
Metals are only found in groups 1 and 2, while every element from group 3 onwards is a non-metal
Metals fill the left and central regions, non-metals cluster in the upper right, with metalloids along the stepped dividing line
questions.explanation: Most elements are metals, and they occupy the left-hand and central blocks; the relatively few non-metals sit in the upper right, separated from the metals by a staircase line of metalloids such as silicon and germanium. The reversed version is tempting for students who remember a 'staircase' but not which side is which — checking a familiar element helps, since sodium (far left) is clearly a metal and oxygen (upper right) clearly is not. Cue: the metallic character increases going left and down.

questions.stem: In group 17, fluorine reacts more vigorously than iodine. Which statement explains this trend correctly?
options: Fluorine holds the most outer-shell electrons in group 17, so it attracts extra electrons most strongly
Fluorine loses its seven outer electrons most easily, so it reacts fastest of all the halogens
Fluorine's outer shell is closest to the nucleus, so an incoming electron is attracted most strongly
Iodine's outer shell is closest to the nucleus, so it captures an incoming electron most strongly
questions.explanation: Halogens react by gaining one electron, and fluorine's outer shell is nearest the nucleus with least shielding, so it pulls in that electron most strongly — reactivity therefore decreases down group 17, the opposite of group 1. The option about fluorine losing seven electrons is tempting for students who apply the group 1 rule everywhere, but non-metals on the right of the table gain electrons rather than lose them. Cue: check whether the element is a metal or a non-metal before deciding which way the reactivity trend runs.

questions.stem: An element X has the electron arrangement 2,8,7. Which set of predictions about X is correct?
options: Group 17, period 7, a non-metal that gains seven electrons to form an ion with a 7- charge
Group 3, period 17, a metalloid that shares its outer electrons without forming ions
Group 17, period 3, a non-metal that gains one electron to form an ion with a 1- charge
Group 7, period 3, a metal that loses seven electrons to form an ion with a 7+ charge
questions.explanation: Three occupied shells put X in period 3, and seven outer electrons put it in group 17 (the halogens), so it is a non-metal that completes its outer shell by gaining one electron, giving a 1- ion. The 'group 7, loses seven electrons' option is the common trap: it uses the older group numbering and then wrongly treats a right-hand non-metal as a metal. Cue: with seven valence electrons, gaining one is far easier than losing seven.

questions.stem: Group 18 elements (helium, neon, argon) barely react. Why, in terms of atomic structure?
options: Their atoms have a full outer shell, so little tendency to gain or share electrons
Their atoms have an empty outer shell, so no electrons are free to bond
Their nuclei hold equal protons and neutrons, making the atoms stable
Their atoms are the largest in each period, so their outer electrons are held loosely
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions involve the outer-shell electrons, and a filled outer shell is a very stable arrangement, so noble gas atoms have almost no driving force to react. The 'empty outer shell' option sounds similar but is wrong: helium's outer shell holds 2 electrons and neon's holds 8 — they are full, not empty. Also note that stability here is chemical (electron arrangement), not nuclear (proton and neutron numbers), and noble gas atoms are among the smaller atoms in each period.

questions.stem: Going down group 1 from lithium to rubidium, what happens to atomic size, and why?
options: Radius increases, because extra neutrons make the nucleus much larger
Radius stays the same, because every atom has one outer electron
Radius increases, because each element has one more occupied shell
Radius decreases, because rising nuclear charge pulls electrons closer
questions.explanation: Each new period adds another occupied electron shell, so the outermost electrons sit further from the nucleus and the atom is bigger. The 'increasing nuclear charge' option describes the trend that operates across a period, where no new shell is added; down a group the extra shell outweighs the extra nuclear charge. The cue is the direction: down a group think shells, across a period think nuclear pull.

questions.stem: An atom of an element has the electron arrangement 2,8,8,1. Where is this element found in the periodic table?
options: Group 1, period 4
Group 1, period 3
Group 8, period 4
Group 4, period 1
questions.explanation: The group number for main-group elements comes from the number of outer-shell electrons (here 1), and the period number comes from the number of occupied shells (here 4). 'Group 1, period 3' is the common slip of counting only the full shells and ignoring the outermost one. Always count every occupied shell for the period, including the partly filled outer shell.

questions.stem: An element sits in group 2, period 3 of the periodic table. Which set of predictions about a neutral atom of this element is correct?
options: It is a non-metal with 2 occupied shells and 3 outer electrons, and forms a 2+ ion
It is a metal with 3 occupied shells and 2 outer electrons, and forms a 2+ ion
It is a metal with 2 occupied shells and 3 outer electrons, and forms a 3+ ion
It is a non-metal with 3 occupied shells and 2 outer electrons, and forms a 2− ion
questions.explanation: Group 2 means two outer-shell electrons and period 3 means three occupied shells; elements on the far left of the table are metals, and metals lose their outer electrons, so this atom forms a 2+ ion. The option swapping the numbers (2 shells, 3 outer electrons) mixes up the two rules — group gives outer electrons, period gives shells. A quick check: any element in groups 1 or 2 is a metal, so a 2− ion is not possible here.

questions.stem: In the modern periodic table, the elements are placed in a definite order from hydrogen onwards. What quantity increases by one from each element to the next?
options: The number of protons in the nucleus
The relative atomic mass of the atom
The number of neutrons in the nucleus
The number of occupied electron shells
questions.explanation: Each element is defined by its atomic number, the number of protons, and the table is built in order of increasing atomic number, so it rises by one at every step. Ordering by relative atomic mass is tempting because Mendeleev originally used mass, but mass does not increase step by step in every case (tellurium is heavier than iodine yet comes first), and it is not what defines an element. Neutron numbers vary between isotopes and do not follow a steady pattern, and the number of shells only increases when you start a new row.

questions.stem: Where are the transition metals found in the periodic table, and what type of elements are they?
options: In the block on the far right of the table, and they are all metals
In the central block between groups 2 and 13, and they are all non-metals
In the two detached rows at the bottom, and they are all non-metals
In the central block between groups 2 and 13, and they are all metals
questions.explanation: The transition metals occupy the wide central block that sits between group 2 on the left and group 13 on the right, and every element in that block is a metal, including iron, copper and zinc. Placing them on the far right confuses them with the non-metals and noble gases, which occupy that region. The two detached rows at the bottom are the lanthanoids and actinoids, which are also metals rather than non-metals.

questions.stem: How do the elements change as you move from left to right across period 3, from sodium to argon?
options: Metallic character stays the same, since all period 3 elements are metals
Metallic character stays the same, since all period 3 elements are non-metals
Metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases
Metallic character increases and non-metallic character decreases
questions.explanation: A row begins with reactive metals on the left and ends with non-metals and a noble gas on the right, so metallic character falls and non-metallic character rises across the row. The reversed option describes the trend going right to left, or the trend down a group, not across a period. Period 3 clearly contains both metals (sodium, magnesium, aluminium) and non-metals (phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, argon), so neither 'all metals' option can be true.

questions.stem: Four atoms have the electron arrangements 2,8,6 (element W), 2,8,8,2 (element X), 2,8,8,6 (element Y) and 2,8,1 (element Z). Which two elements would be expected to have the most similar chemical properties?
options: W and X, because both have three occupied electron shells
X and Y, because both have four occupied electron shells
Y and Z, because both are found on the left of the table
W and Y, because both have six electrons in the outer shell
questions.explanation: Chemical behaviour is governed mainly by the number of outer-shell electrons, and elements with the same number sit in the same group, so the two atoms with six outer electrons behave alike. Choosing the pair with the same number of shells confuses periods with groups: elements in the same row have different outer-electron counts and quite different chemistry. The pair with four shells also share only a period, and an atom with six outer electrons is a non-metal on the right, not on the left.

questions.stem: A sodium atom (2,8,1) is considerably larger than a chlorine atom (2,8,7), even though both are in period 3. Why?
options: Sodium is a metal, and metal atoms are always larger than non-metal atoms regardless of their position
Chlorine has six more protons pulling on the same third shell, so that shell is drawn in closer
Chlorine has six more electrons, and the extra electrons repel each other and spread the atom out further
Sodium has fewer occupied shells, and fewer shells always means a smaller nucleus but a larger electron cloud
questions.explanation: Both atoms use three shells, but chlorine's nucleus carries 17 protons compared with sodium's 11, so the stronger attraction pulls the outer shell in and the atom is smaller. The repulsion argument sounds reasonable but the extra nuclear charge outweighs the extra electron repulsion, which is why radius falls across every period. Sodium and chlorine have the same number of occupied shells, and 'metals are always larger' fails when you compare across different periods, such as caesium with a small metal like beryllium.

questions.stem: Which properties are typical of most non-metals at room temperature?
options: Good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, all solid
Good conductors of electricity but not heat, shiny, several liquid
Poor conductors of electricity, malleable, very high melting points
Poor conductors of heat and electricity, brittle, several are gases
questions.explanation: Non-metals generally lack the free-moving delocalised electrons that let metals conduct, so they are poor conductors, and their solids shatter rather than bend; many (such as oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine) are gases. The set describing good conductors that are malleable is the classic description of metals, not non-metals. Cue: brittle plus poor conductor points to non-metal; malleable plus good conductor points to metal.

questions.stem: In which directions across the periodic table does metallic character generally increase?
options: Up a group and to the left across a period
Down a group and to the left across a period
Up a group and to the right across a period
Down a group and to the right across a period
questions.explanation: Metallic character depends on how easily an atom loses outer electrons; atoms get larger down a group so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more easily lost, and atoms on the left of a period have few outer electrons to lose. The reverse answer (up a group and to the right) describes increasing non-metallic character, which is why it feels plausible. Cue: the most metallic elements sit at the bottom left (caesium, francium), the most non-metallic at the top right.

questions.stem: Four neutral atoms are considered: fluorine, chlorine, sodium and magnesium. Which atom is the largest, and why?
options: Sodium, because it is in period 3 and has only one outer electron, held loosely far from the nucleus
Chlorine, because it has more electrons than sodium and so needs more room to hold them
Fluorine, because it is at the top of group 17 and gains electrons more readily than the others
Magnesium, because it has two outer electrons and therefore a larger outer shell than sodium
questions.explanation: Atomic size increases down a group (more shells) and decreases from left to right across a period (the growing nuclear charge pulls the same shell in tighter), so among these the period 3 element furthest to the left — sodium — is largest. Chlorine tempts students who assume more electrons means a bigger atom, but chlorine's 17 protons pull its third shell in far more tightly than sodium's 11 protons do. Cue: compare period first (more shells wins), then position across the row.

questions.stem: Period 1 holds only hydrogen and helium; period 2 holds eight. Why is period 1 so short?
options: They are the only elements that are gases at room temperature
They have no neutrons, so only two such light elements can exist
The first shell holds only two electrons, so a third starts a new period
The period number gives outer shell capacity, so these hold one each
questions.explanation: The length of each row is set by how many electrons fit in the shells being filled: the first shell holds only 2, so lithium's third electron starts the second shell and therefore the second row. The idea that the period number tells you the outer shell capacity is a muddled version of the real rule — the period number tells you how many shells are in use, not how many electrons each holds. A useful cue: row number = number of occupied electron shells, and shell capacities (2, then 8) set the row lengths.

questions.stem: What is the charge on a proton?
options: Positive
Negative
Neutral
It varies
questions.explanation: Protons carry a positive charge, electrons an equal negative one, and neutrons none. An atom is neutral overall because it holds equal numbers of protons and electrons.
questions.teaching:
An atom has three kinds of particle in it, and each carries a fixed electrical charge that never varies. Two of them are charged and one is not.

The particles in the nucleus and the ones orbiting outside it carry opposite charges, which is exactly why the atom holds together — opposite charges attract, and that attraction is what keeps electrons bound rather than flying off. The neutron is the odd one out, carrying nothing at all, which is where its name comes from. Getting the signs the right way round matters later: it is the reason a nucleus repels another nucleus, and the reason losing an electron leaves an atom with an overall charge.

questions.stem: Where are electrons found in an atom?
options: Evenly spread through the atom
Only on the atom's surface
In shells around the nucleus
Inside the nucleus itself
questions.explanation: Electrons occupy shells, or energy levels, around the nucleus. Placing them inside the nucleus is the common error — the nucleus holds only protons and neutrons.
questions.teaching:
Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into a nucleus that occupies almost none of its volume. If a nucleus were a marble on the centre circle of the MCG, the atom would stretch to the outer fence.

Everything in between is where the electrons are. They are not scattered randomly through it, and they are not mixed in with the nucleus — they occupy defined energy levels, often drawn as rings, each holding up to a set number before the next one starts. The outermost of those levels is the one that does all the chemistry, because it is the only part of the atom that ever meets another atom.

questions.stem: What does an element's atomic number tell you?
options: The number of protons
The number of neutrons
The total number of particles
The mass of one atom
questions.explanation: The atomic number is the proton count, and it is what makes an element that element. Neutron number can vary between isotopes of the same element without changing which element it is.
questions.teaching:
The periodic table is ordered by one thing, and it is not mass. Each element gets its position from a count of particles in the nucleus — specifically the positively charged ones, because that count fixes the element's identity and, through the matching electrons, all of its chemistry.

Mass number is what people confuse it with. That adds the neutrons in as well, so it tells you how heavy a particular atom is rather than what it is. Two atoms of the same element can have different mass numbers and still be the same element; alter the other count and you have moved to a different square on the table entirely.

questions.stem: What do elements in the same group of the periodic table share?
options: Similar chemical properties
The same number of neutrons
The same atomic mass
The same physical state
questions.explanation: A group is a column, and its members have the same number of outer electrons, which is what gives them similar chemistry. Mass and physical state vary widely down a group — think helium against radon.
questions.teaching:
The periodic table is not just a list in order of size. Its shape is deliberate: elements are arranged so that ones behaving alike end up stacked in the same column.

The reason sits in the outer electrons. Everything in a column has the same number of electrons in its outermost shell, and since that shell is the only part involved in bonding, they react in similar ways. It is why every element in one particular column fizzes in water and every element in another refuses to react with anything. Note what they do not share: mass, size and physical state vary enormously down a column — helium and radon sit in the same one.

questions.stem: What is an isotope?
options: An atom with the usual protons but different neutrons
An atom that has lost or gained one or more electrons
An atom of a completely different element
An atom joined to another by a covalent bond
questions.explanation: Isotopes of an element have the same proton count but different numbers of neutrons, so they differ in mass. An atom that has lost or gained electrons is an ion, which is the usual confusion.
questions.teaching:
Every element is defined by one number: how many protons sit in its nucleus. Carbon is carbon because it has six of them, and change that count and you no longer have carbon at all.

Neutrons are the loose variable. They add mass and they affect how stable a nucleus is, but they play no part in deciding which element you have. So one element can turn up in several versions that weigh slightly different amounts while behaving identically in every chemical reaction. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are the same element doing the same chemistry — the difference sits in the nucleus, not in how the atom bonds. Watch out for the near-miss: an atom that has lost or gained an electron is a different idea again, and it has its own name.

questions.stem: What holds the atoms in a compound together?
options: Friction
Chemical bonds
Gravity
Magnetism
questions.explanation: Atoms in a compound are held by chemical bonds, formed as electrons are shared or transferred. Gravity acts between all masses but is far too weak at this scale to matter.
questions.teaching:
A compound is not a mixture. Sand and salt stirred together can be separated with water and a filter; a compound cannot, because its atoms are genuinely joined and only a chemical reaction will part them.

What joins them is electrons. Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell, and they reach one either by transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing pairs between them. Both arrangements create a strong attraction that has to be broken by a reaction. Gravity is far too weak to matter at this scale, and magnetism is a different force entirely — the joining is electrical, and it happens through the outer electrons.

questions.stem: What is the charge on an electron?
options: It varies
Negative
Positive
Neutral
questions.explanation: Electrons carry a negative charge equal and opposite to a proton's. That balance is why a complete atom has no overall charge.
questions.teaching:
Electrons are tiny compared with the particles in the nucleus — around 1/1836 of a proton's mass — but electrically they are its exact counterweight.

That equal-and-opposite pairing is the whole reason ordinary matter is electrically neutral: an atom holds the same number of each, and the charges cancel. Disturb the balance and you get an ion. Strip an electron away and the atom is left short of negative charge, so it becomes positive overall; add one and it becomes negative. Static electricity, batteries and every circuit in your house are all built on electrons moving while the nuclei stay put.

questions.stem: Which particles are found in the nucleus?
options: Electrons only
Protons and neutrons
Protons and electrons
Neutrons and electrons
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons sit outside it in shells. Putting electrons in the nucleus is the most common structural error.
questions.teaching:
An atom has three particle types, and they are not evenly distributed. Two of them sit packed together in a dense centre; the third occupies the huge, nearly empty space around it.

The two in the centre are the heavy ones, and between them they account for essentially all of the atom's mass. One of them is charged and one is not. The particle outside is the light one, and it is the one that moves between atoms during chemistry — which is why the nucleus is untouched by ordinary chemical reactions. Changing what is in the nucleus is nuclear physics, not chemistry, and it takes vastly more energy.

questions.stem: What is the mass number of an atom?
options: Protons plus neutrons
Protons only
Protons plus electrons
Neutrons only
questions.explanation: Mass number counts the particles in the nucleus, since electrons weigh almost nothing. The proton count on its own is the atomic number, which is the near-miss.
questions.teaching:
Two numbers get quoted for an atom and they are easy to mix up, so it helps to know what each is counting.

One counts only the positively charged particles, and it is what fixes the element's identity — change it and you have a different element. The other is a count of everything heavy in the nucleus, so it includes the uncharged particles as well. Electrons are left out of both, because they weigh so little that they make no measurable difference. This is why two atoms of the same element can have different values for the second number while sharing the first: they are isotopes, differing only in how many uncharged particles they carry.

questions.stem: What is a row of the periodic table called?
options: A family
A period
A group
A shell
questions.explanation: Rows are periods and columns are groups. Elements in a period share the number of electron shells; elements in a group share outer electrons and so share chemistry.
questions.teaching:
The table has rows and columns, and they mean different things, so the two names are worth keeping straight.

Reading across a row, each element has one more proton than the last, and the outer electron shell gradually fills up. When it is full the row ends and a new one begins with the next shell. So a row tells you how many shells an atom has, and the row number matches that count. Reading down a column, elements share the number of electrons in that outer shell, which is why they behave alike chemically. Rows are about how many shells; columns are about what is in the outermost one.

questions.stem: What are the group 1 metals called?
options: The halogens
The transition metals
The alkali metals
The noble gases
questions.explanation: Group 1 holds the alkali metals — lithium, sodium, potassium — which react vigorously with water. The halogens are group 17 and the noble gases group 18, at the other end of the table.
questions.teaching:
Several columns of the table have names that get used more often than their numbers, and they describe how the elements behave.

The first column holds soft, light metals that react violently with water, giving off hydrogen and leaving a solution that turns indicator blue — that is, a base or alkali, which is where the family name comes from. The reactions get more violent as you go down: lithium fizzes, sodium skitters, and caesium is genuinely dangerous. Two other families are worth knowing by name: the very unreactive gases in the last column, and the highly reactive non-metals in the column just before it.

questions.stem: Why is an atom electrically neutral?
options: It has equal protons and electrons
It has no charged particles at all
Its neutrons cancel out the protons
Its electrons carry no charge
questions.explanation: Equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons cancel exactly. An atom certainly does contain charged particles — they simply balance, which is the distinction being tested.
questions.teaching:
It is worth being precise here, because the obvious answer is wrong. A neutral atom is not one with no charged particles in it — it is full of them.

The point is that they balance. Every positive particle in the nucleus is matched by a negative one outside it, so the charges add up to zero even though nothing has been removed. Neutrons play no part in this at all; they are uncharged, so they cannot cancel anything. The balance can be broken: gain or lose electrons and the atom becomes an ion with an overall charge. That is a change to the electron count, never to the nucleus.
